analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale, manufacture, and transfer of all handguns, leaving them only to police, the military, and licensed shooting clubs.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for anyone to import, make, sell, buy, or transfer a handgun in the United States. Exceptions would cover the armed forces, police and other government agencies, and private shooting clubs licensed by the Treasury Department, which would keep members' handguns locked up at the club. Current owners could turn in their handguns to law enforcement and be paid at least the gun's market value. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the bill's stated aim was to cut handgun homicides, armed robberies, and shootings by removing handguns from ordinary commerce; the bill's own findings argue a national restriction on non-police, non-military handguns would significantly reduce violent crime. People turning in handguns would be reimbursed at fair market value.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that handguns are used disproportionately in homicide, aggravated assault, and armed robbery, and that a national restriction on non-law-enforcement handguns would significantly reduce violent gun deaths [S3].

It makes it unlawful for anyone to import, manufacture, sell, buy, transfer, receive, or transport a handgun, with exceptions for the U.S. armed forces, federal and state agencies, unserviceable collector guns, and Treasury-licensed pistol clubs [S2].
Current owners could voluntarily deliver handguns to a designated law enforcement agency and be reimbursed the greater of fair market value or $25, paid from license fees and federal revenues [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of existing handgun owners, who could keep guns only by joining and storing them at a licensed pistol club; the firearms industry, which would lose the civilian handgun market; and taxpayers, who would fund buybacks beyond what license fees cover.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: The bill would end the sale of new handguns entirely and restrict private ownership to licensed clubs, eliminating handgun ownership in the home; the bill itself concedes that defensive purposes would have to be 'adequately accomplished by other means' [S3].

The $25 reimbursement floor is far below what many handguns were worth; owners who did not surrender their guns would possess firearms that could be seized and forfeited if used or intended for use in any violation [S3].
The bill defines 'handgun' by a barrel under ten inches and one-handed firing design, a definition critics would argue sweeps in firearms that are not typically concealable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it had become law, the tradeoff would have been a drastic reduction in handgun availability — the bill's stated goal of lower gun violence — against the removal of handgun ownership from tens of millions of households and the near-elimination of the civilian handgun market. The proposal was an outlier even among gun-control proposals of its era: it drew no cosponsors and was never taken up by any committee or chamber.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee two days after introduction, sent to its Crime subcommittee two days after that, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Sidney Yates introduced the Handgun Control Act of 1989 on May 24, 1989 [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day, and to that committee's Subcommittee on Crime on May 26, 1989 [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never left the subcommittee, never got a hearing, and never came to a floor vote in either chamber [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors for its entire two-year life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing handgun owners and the firearms industry are better off: the bill never advanced, so handgun sales, manufacturing, and private ownership continued unchanged. Supporters of stricter gun laws gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

for.name: Rep. Sidney R. Yates
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Handgun Control Act of 1989 and shepherded it as its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee / Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the Crime subcommittee received it on May 26, 1989, and no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Organized opposition to handgun-ban proposals of this era, which kept such measures from advancing even in a Democratic-controlled Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded supporter was its Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party, so no party-line pattern can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have banned the import, manufacture, sale, and transfer of all civilian handguns, ending the domestic handgun market except for sales to government agencies. The industry's interest in the bill's failure ran against the bill's stated public-safety goal. Because the bill died, the industry's position is unchanged.

Had it passed, the bill would have made licensed pistol clubs the only private channel for handgun use, with clubs holding members' guns under lock and paying a $25 annual fee — turning them into the permanent gatekeepers of civilian handgun access. It never advanced, so this never took effect.
